qs.q: While tracing the brachial artery, an anatomist notes that it is a continuation of a larger vessel. At which anatomical landmark does the axillary artery officially become the brachial artery?
o: Lateral border of the first rib
Neck of the radius bone shaft
qs.e: The axillary artery begins at the lateral border of the first rib and ends at the inferior border of the teres major, where it continues as the brachial artery. The lateral border of the first rib marks its proximal start, not its transition point.
qs.s: PAT III — Progress Assessment Test (8 November 2019) — Revision Guide: MCQs

qs.q: During a surgical dissection of the axilla, a resident identifies various vascular structures. Which statement about the axillary artery or its major branches is INCORRECT?
o: The thoracodorsal artery is the major blood supply to the latissimus dorsi muscle
The thoracoacromial trunk supplies blood to the deltoid muscle
The lateral thoracic artery supplies blood to the breast
The second part of the axillary artery lies anterior to the pectoralis minor muscle
qs.e: The second part of the axillary artery lies posterior to the pectoralis minor muscle, not anterior to it. The other branches correctly supply their respective regions.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The axillary artery is the continuation of the subclavian artery that supplies the shoulder and upper limb. It runs from the lateral border of the first rib to the lower border of the teres major, where it becomes the brachial artery.

sections.p: The axillary artery is the main conduit for arterial blood to the upper limb, bridging the subclavian and brachial arteries.
b: Length ~10 cm, lies deep to the pectoralis minor
Divided into three parts by the pectoralis minor muscle

sections.p: It begins at the lateral border of the first rib (continuation of the subclavian) and ends at the lower edge of the teres major, becoming the brachial artery.
b: First part: from first rib to medial border of pectoralis minor
Third part: from lateral border of pectoralis minor to teres major

sections.p: The artery is surrounded by important nerves and veins that are clinically relevant during surgery or trauma.
b: Posterior: posterior cord of brachial plexus, axillary vein
Lateral: thoracodorsal nerve, circumflex humeral vessels

sections.p: Branches arise from each part to supply the shoulder girdle, chest wall, and upper limb.
b: Second part: thoracoacromial artery, lateral thoracic artery, subscapular artery
Third part: anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries, profunda brachii

sections.p: The arterial wall receives sympathetic innervation that regulates vasomotor tone.
b: Sympathetic fibers travel with the thoracic sympathetic trunk

sections.p: Delivers oxygen‑rich blood to the shoulder muscles, clavicle, and the entire arm, supporting movement and metabolism.
b: Provides collateral flow via anastomoses with the subscapular and circumflex humeral arteries

sections.p: Injury or disease of the axillary artery can cause limb ischemia, hemorrhage, or neurovascular compromise.
b: Traumatic transection (e.g., high‑energy shoulder injury) → rapid blood loss, need urgent control
Aneurysm (often post‑catheterization) → risk of embolism, compressive neuropathy
Thoracic outlet syndrome → arterial compression, possible thrombosis

t.b: Is there flow obstruction or aneurysm? → shows turbulence, reduced velocity; if unavailable, use clinical pulse exam
What is the exact location and extent of injury? → delineates laceration, pseudo‑aneurysm; if unavailable, plain X‑ray for fracture and clinical exam
Is limb perfusion adequate? → ratio <0.9 suggests significant stenosis; if unavailable, compare bilateral radial pulses

sections.p: Key points to recall for exams and bedside assessment.
b: Remember the three parts are defined by the pectoralis minor muscle
Branches of the second part supply the deltoid and shoulder joint
Injury proximal to the third part can compromise the entire arm

whenToSeekHelp: Severe shoulder trauma with absent distal pulses
Rapidly expanding axillary swelling suggesting aneurysm rupture
Signs of limb ischemia: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia

faq.q: Why is the axillary artery divided into three parts?
faq.a: The pectoralis minor muscle serves as a landmark; each part has distinct branches important for surgical planning.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of axillary artery injury?
faq.a: High‑energy blunt or penetrating trauma to the shoulder, often associated with fractures of the proximal humerus.

faq.q: How can you clinically assess axillary artery patency?
faq.a: Palpate the distal brachial and radial pulses and compare blood pressure between arms.
